column1: # Ground truth for parseColor(), and the one table here whose expected values
# are NOT v1's.
# v1 at tag v9.0.2, commit 890eed2, working tree clean. Generated the same way
# as its siblings -- that generator reproduced all 612 rows of the four original
# tables exactly, which is what establishes it is the same v1 they came from.
# # Why this table records a third answer
# On alpha, **neither v1 nor this implementation is right**, so pinning either
# would pin an artefact. v1 quantises alpha to eight bits and rounds to three
# decimals, so `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1)` parses to `0.102`. Ours round-trips it
# through `f32`, giving `0.10000000149011612`. Both are the float width of an
# internal representation leaking through a public boundary.
# The browser is the tiebreak, as it was for the mix clamp: `getComputedStyle`
# on `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1)` answers `0.1`. The rule is **`parseColor` returns the
# number the author wrote**, and the `a` column carries that. Rows where v1 or
# this surface disagrees are `diverges`, and the note records what each gives.
# **These rows failed on both surfaces when they were written, and that was
# the point** -- they were the failing-first evidence for the finding. As of
# `302c31e` they pass: `parse_channels` presents each channel as the shortest
# decimal identifying its `f32`, and computes a hex alpha as `byte / 255`. The
# `note` column records what v1 still gives, which is what these rows continue
# to diverge from.
# There was no second fix to wait for. The JavaScript surface has no parser of
# its own -- it reads through the addon, which calls `parse_channels` -- so one
# change moved both surfaces at once.
# # What hid it, and what it narrows to
# Nothing anywhere parses a CSS string carrying an alpha -- the colour tests
# build `{r, g, b, a}` objects directly, so the alpha never passes the parser.
# The parameter no row varied, for the fourth time in this audit.
# Hex-byte alphas need their own rule, and two of these three rows are what
# show it. Presenting the `f32` as its shortest identifying decimal fixes the
# decimals and the percentages; a hex byte needs `byte / 255` computed where
# the byte is known, because the ratio is not a decimal any `f32` reaches.
# `#0000007f` and `#0008` are the rows that discriminate: widening gives
# `0.5333333333333333`. **`#000000cc` cannot tell the two apart** -- widening
# gives the shortest decimal for `f32(0.8)`, which is `0.8`, and `204 / 255` is
# also `0.8`. It is here as the row that agrees under both rules, which is the
# same trap as the group whose members agree whether or not the count
# propagates: an implementation checked only against it would report a passing
# branch nothing took.
# Percentage spellings land on the same f32 as their decimal equivalents, so
# `33%` fails exactly as `0.33` does. `12.5%` passes: it is a negative power of
# two and exact in binary32.
# Only three of the six decimal alpha rows fail on this surface: `0.5`, `0.25` and
# `0.75` are exactly representable in binary32 and already read back correctly.
# It is `0.1`, `0.33` and `0.9` that do not -- which is why an eye passing over
# the round numbers would have called it fine.
# # The css column is quoted, and that is not decoration
# A hex colour starts with `#`, which is this format's comment character, so
# `#808080` as a bare first field is dropped by both walkers' own comment
# filter -- silently, leaving a table that looks complete and tests three fewer
# rows than it lists. This file lost three rows that way before the count was
# checked against the generator's. Quoting follows `ellipsis.tsv`, which quotes
# its strings for the same reason.
